Sound decisions for companies that have outgrown the way they run.

Larch & Vale is a small Canadian consulting practice. We work with owners and leadership teams of privately held companies on strategy, operating structure, and the habits that keep both honest.

Owner-led clients

Privately held and family-owned companies in the middle market.

A small senior team

The people on the first call are the people doing the work.

Fixed scope

Deliverables and price agreed before we begin.

Four kinds of work, one way of doing it.

Strategy and planning

A written strategy the whole leadership team can repeat, including the choices about where not to compete.

Read more

Operating model and organization

Roles, reporting lines and decision rights that match how the company actually makes its money.

Read more

Performance management

A monthly rhythm of numbers and conversations that brings problems up while they are still small.

Read more

Leadership and transition support

Succession planning, onboarding for new executives, and the first months after an ownership change.

Read more

Advice you can act on the following Monday.

Plain language

Reports are short and written for the person who has to decide.

Your people in the room

Your managers help build the answer, so it holds after we leave.

A defined end

Every engagement has a finish date and a handover, not a retainer by default.

Sample engagements

Second-generation owners, regional distributor

Sample engagement (illustrative, not a real client)

A founder and two successors disagreed about which product lines to keep. A three-week review of margins and customer overlap gave them a shared set of facts, and we facilitated the decision.

Partner succession, professional services firm

Sample engagement (illustrative, not a real client)

Two senior partners planned to step back within five years. We mapped client relationships, agreed a transition schedule, and set out what each successor would take on first.

Recent thinking

All insights

Start with a conversation.

A first call takes thirty minutes and costs nothing. Bring the question you keep coming back to.

LVP_HOME; $C['services'] = <<<'LVP_SERVICES'

What we do, and what it looks like in practice.

Four areas of work. Most engagements touch more than one, and we scope them so you know the deliverables and the price before we start.

Strategy and planning

We help the leadership team decide where the company will compete over the next three to five years, and write it down in a form people can use.

Typical deliverables

  • A strategy document of ten pages or fewer
  • A short list of priorities with named owners
  • A one-year plan tied to the budget

Typical duration: six to ten weeks.

Operating model and organization

As companies grow, reporting lines and decisions pile up around a few people. We map how work and decisions actually move, then redesign what is not working.

Typical deliverables

  • Current-state map of roles and decision rights
  • Proposed structure with transition steps
  • Role descriptions for the changed positions

Typical duration: eight to twelve weeks.

Performance management

Many owners see the numbers late and discuss them rarely. We set up a monthly cycle that is short enough to keep and specific enough to act on.

Typical deliverables

  • A one-page scorecard in your own numbers
  • A meeting calendar and standing agendas
  • Training for the managers who run the cycle

Typical duration: six weeks, followed by two review sessions.

Leadership and transition support

Ownership changes, retirements and new executive hires all stress a company. We work with the people involved, before and after the change.

Typical deliverables

  • A succession and handover plan
  • A 90-day onboarding plan for a new executive
  • Facilitated sessions for owners and successors

Typical duration: varies with the scope.

Three ways to work with us

Fixed-scope project

A defined question, a defined set of deliverables, one price.

Advisory days

A block of days used as needed, for leaders who want a sounding board.

Interim support

A senior person embedded for a limited period to lead a change you have already decided on.

Not sure which one fits?

Describe the situation in a few lines. We will tell you honestly whether we are the right people to help.

LVP_SERVICES; $C['approach'] = <<<'LVP_APPROACH'

A method that fits on one page.

Every engagement follows the same four steps. The length of each step changes. The order does not.

Listen

Weeks one and two

We interview owners, managers and a sample of staff, and read the documents you already have. We ask what has been tried before and why it stopped.

Diagnose

Weeks two to four

We separate symptoms from causes and test our reading with the numbers. You receive a short written diagnosis before any recommendation is made.

Decide

Weeks four to six

We set out two or three realistic options with their costs and risks. Your leadership team chooses, and we record the reasoning.

Hand over

The final weeks

We help put the decision into practice, train the people who will own it, and leave you with documents that make sense without us.

What we ask of you

  • A named sponsor with authority to decide
  • Access to the people and numbers we need, within the first week
  • Honest feedback on drafts, including the parts you dislike

See whether the method suits your question.

Tell us what you are facing. A first call costs nothing.

A small practice, on purpose.

Larch & Vale is a Canadian management consulting practice for privately held companies. We keep the team small so that senior people do the work.

How we work

Most of our clients are owner-led businesses that grew faster than their management systems. They do not need a hundred-page report. They need someone to look closely, say what they see, and help them decide.

We take on a small number of engagements at a time. Each one has a named lead, a fixed scope and a date when we stop.

What we hold to

Respect the room

Know when to stop

LVP_CONTACT; $PO[0] = ['slug'=>'strategy-papers-nobody-reads','title'=>"Why strategy documents stop being read",'excerpt'=>"Most strategy papers fail on length, not on quality. A ten-page limit changes what gets written, and who reads it.",'content'=><<<'LVPOST_0'

A strategy paper is usually finished in a burst of effort and filed a week later. The usual explanation is a lack of follow-through. We think the cause is simpler: the paper is too long to be used.

Length forces choices

When a document has to fit on ten pages, the authors must decide what matters most. That argument is the useful part of the exercise. A hundred-page paper lets everyone keep their favourite project and avoid the decision.

Write for the person who has to act

A branch manager does not need the market analysis. She needs to know what changes in her quarter. Write that section first, in plain words, and let the supporting material sit in an appendix.

Test it out loud

Ask three managers to describe the strategy in two minutes without notes. If the answers differ, the paper has not done its job yet.

Sample article for the demo build.

LVPOST_0]; $PO[1] = ['slug'=>'decision-rights-one-page-test','title'=>"Decision rights: a one-page test for your leadership team",'excerpt'=>"If two managers can each say they were meant to decide, nobody decided. A short exercise shows where this happens.",'content'=><<<'LVPOST_1'

Growing companies rarely write down who decides what. The founder decides everything early on, and later the habit spreads informally. Then a hire, a price change or a supplier switch is made twice, or not at all.

The exercise

List ten recurring decisions on a page: pricing exceptions, hiring below director level, capital spending over a set amount, and so on. Ask each member of the leadership team to write the name of the person who decides each one.

What to look for

Compare the pages. Where answers match, leave things alone. Where they differ, you have found a gap. Where one name appears on every line, you have found a bottleneck.

Fix the gaps first. Bottlenecks take longer, because they usually depend on trust that has to be built.

Sample article for the demo build.

LVPOST_1]; $PO[2] = ['slug'=>'after-an-ownership-change','title'=>"The first months after an ownership change",'excerpt'=>"Staff read every signal in the first weeks. A few early, visible decisions matter more than a long communication plan.",'content'=><<<'LVPOST_2'

After a sale, a succession or a new investor, employees watch the new owners closely. They are looking for answers to a short list of questions: will my job change, who decides now, and what will be different.

Answer the obvious questions early

Say what is not changing, in the first week and in plain terms. People tolerate change they can see coming. They struggle with silence.

Make a few decisions visibly

Pick two or three pending decisions and settle them quickly. A delayed approval that finally moves tells staff more than any announcement.

Keep the old rhythm for a while

Existing meetings and reports give people something steady. Change them one at a time, and say why.

Sample article for the demo build.
